Newborn Care

Kernicterus: severe newborn jaundice and urgent warning signs

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Newborn jaundice is common; kernicterus is rare and serious. Prompt bilirubin testing and appropriate treatment can prevent much of this harm. A jaundiced baby who is unusually sleepy, difficult to wake, not feeding, floppy or stiff needs immediate emergency assessment, not an extra feed and a wait.

Jaundice, acute toxicity and kernicterus are different

Bilirubin is a yellow pigment produced when red blood cells break down. The liver processes it for removal. Newborns may produce more bilirubin than their immature processing and elimination can handle, causing yellow skin or eyes. Jaundice is not itself proof of brain injury, and most affected babies do not develop kernicterus.

Very high unconjugated bilirubin can enter the brain and cause acute bilirubin encephalopathy. Kernicterus usually refers to the lasting neurological injury that can follow. Acute warning signs do not automatically establish permanent damage, but urgent treatment is essential to prevent or limit injury. Do not wait for every sign to appear.

Warning signs: when to get immediate help

Get immediate emergency help if a baby with jaundice is harder to wake or sleepier than usual, is not feeding, is floppy or stiff, has jerking movements or a seizure, or has breathing difficulty or pauses. An unusual high-pitched or inconsolable cry, arching the head or back, abnormal eye movements or reduced responsiveness also require immediate assessment.

With jaundice, a temperature of 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower, or no wet nappies, also needs emergency help. Jaundice in the first 24 hours requires immediate hospital assessment. Do not drive yourself with an unwell baby; arrange another driver or emergency transport. Vomiting, fewer wet or dirty nappies, worsening yellow colour or reduced feeding are concerning: obtain urgent same-day advice, and use emergency care if the severe signs above are present.

Why indirect and direct bilirubin matter

Unconjugated, or indirect, bilirubin travels largely attached to albumin in the blood. The liver conjugates it into a more water-soluble form for excretion through bile and the bowel. Unbound unconjugated bilirubin is the main concern in bilirubin-related brain toxicity; vulnerability also depends on the baby’s maturity and illness.

Conjugated, or direct, bilirubin is not the usual cause of kernicterus, but an elevated direct result is not harmless: it can indicate liver or bile-flow disease. Pale stools or dark urine need prompt assessment. Clinicians consider the bilirubin fractions and the whole situation; treatment charts use total serum bilirubin without simply subtracting the direct fraction.

Causes and babies needing closer monitoring

Risk increases with lower gestational age, jaundice appearing early, bilirubin rising quickly or close to a treatment threshold, previous phototherapy, significant bruising and inadequate milk intake. A parent or sibling who required jaundice treatment or an inherited blood disorder can be relevant. G6PD deficiency can cause increased red-cell breakdown; a baby can deteriorate without an obvious family history.

Rh or ABO antibodies can destroy a baby’s red cells and increase bilirubin. A mother being Rh-negative or blood group O alone does not mean the baby will develop severe jaundice: the baby’s group, maternal antibodies and actual findings matter. Antenatal screening and anti-D prevention where indicated reduce Rh-related disease; they do not prevent every cause of jaundice. Infection, clinical instability and low albumin can increase vulnerability to toxicity.

Rare inherited conditions and older patients

Crigler–Najjar syndrome impairs the enzyme that conjugates bilirubin. Type 1 has absent activity and is particularly severe; type 2 has reduced activity and is usually less severe. It needs specialist lifelong planning, and serious unconjugated bilirubin problems can extend beyond infancy. Bilirubin brain toxicity is predominantly a newborn problem, but it should not be described as impossible in an older person with a severe disorder.

Gilbert syndrome usually causes mild, intermittent unconjugated bilirubin elevation and is different from severe Crigler–Najjar disease. Dubin–Johnson and Rotor syndromes mainly involve conjugated bilirubin handling and are not the usual causes of kernicterus; Rotor can raise both fractions. New or unexplained jaundice in an older child or adult still needs medical assessment rather than a guessed inherited diagnosis.

Medication review, including sulfonamides

Some medicines can displace bilirubin from albumin or trigger haemolysis in susceptible infants. Sulfonamides, including sulfamethoxazole in trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, deserve specific review. Product information contraindicates this combination in infants younger than two months; do not give leftover or unprescribed antibiotics to a newborn.

Breastfeeding exposure is a different decision from giving a medicine directly to the baby. LactMed advises alternatives when the infant is jaundiced, ill, stressed or premature and avoidance when breastfeeding a G6PD-deficient infant; use after the newborn period in a healthy full-term infant may be acceptable. This is a risk-based precaution, not proof that every exposure causes kernicterus. Tell the prescriber about the baby’s condition and all medicines and herbal products; obtain prompt advice rather than stopping necessary treatment yourself.

Testing looks beyond skin colour

Yellowing can be harder to recognise on darker skin, and appearance cannot measure severity. A transcutaneous meter estimates bilirubin through the skin; a blood sample measures total serum bilirubin. A high or near-treatment skin reading needs confirmation according to the local protocol. Babies in their first 24 hours or born before 35 weeks of gestation need serum testing rather than reliance on a skin meter.

Neither a skin reading nor one blood number alone diagnoses kernicterus. Treatment decisions use age in hours, gestational age, serum results and neurotoxicity risks, plus examination and the trend. There is no universal safe or dangerous cutoff for all newborns. Depending on the findings, testing may investigate blood-group antibodies, anaemia, G6PD deficiency, infection or liver disease. Imaging or specialist hearing and neurological assessment may be needed if injury is suspected.

Phototherapy and emergency treatment

Medical phototherapy uses appropriate light to change bilirubin into forms the body can eliminate more easily. The clinical team supervises exposure, eye protection, temperature, hydration and repeat blood tests. Sunlight through a window or outdoors is not a safe substitute; do not delay treatment for sunlight, herbs, water or sugar water. Home phototherapy is suitable only for selected babies under a prescribed monitoring plan.

Dangerously high or rising bilirubin, or signs of significant acute encephalopathy, may require intensive care and an urgent exchange transfusion to remove bilirubin and affected blood cells. Some babies need intravenous fluids; immunoglobulin is reserved for selected immune haemolysis cases because benefit is uncertain and there are risks. These are specialist decisions, not treatments to choose from a home bilirubin chart.

Feeding support helps but does not replace treatment

Effective regular milk intake helps bowel movements carry bilirubin out of the body. Breastfeeding is often offered around 8–12 times in 24 hours in the early days, with feeding and milk-transfer assessment rather than a rigid target alone. Check weight, hydration and age-appropriate nappies with the team; ask for help with latch, expressing or bottle feeding when needed.

If intake is inadequate, a clinician may recommend expressed milk, suitable donor milk or formula supplementation while supporting breastfeeding where desired. Do not withhold needed supplementation or assume more feeds alone will treat dangerous bilirubin levels. A baby too sleepy to feed or not feeding needs emergency assessment. Feeding, phototherapy and other treatment may need to happen together.

Long-term effects and preventing further harm

Established kernicterus can cause involuntary movements and abnormal muscle tone, dyskinetic cerebral palsy, coordination or speech difficulties, hearing loss or auditory neuropathy, impaired upward eye movement and tooth-enamel changes. Some children have learning or intellectual difficulties, but not every child has every feature. Individual developmental assessment is more useful than assuming a fixed outcome.

Urgent treatment aims to prevent or limit injury; it cannot be promised to reverse established permanent damage. Longer-term care can include neurology, hearing and vision services, rehabilitation, communication and feeding support and dental care. Before discharge, know the bilirubin result, whether and when it must be rechecked, the follow-up appointment and emergency signs. Follow-up may be needed after phototherapy because bilirubin can rise again. Seek help sooner if the baby changes, without waiting for the appointment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The AAP 2022 guideline for infants born at least 35 weeks remains current; its implementation FAQ was updated July 2025. Treatment and follow-up depend on age, gestation, measured bilirubin and risk.

Current NHS newborn-jaundice advice supports immediate emergency escalation for the warning signs described. NICE guidance rejects sunlight treatment and requires age-appropriate bilirubin assessment.

Primary genetic and medication information distinguishes severe unconjugated disorders from generally milder inherited jaundice and separates infant dosing from breastfeeding exposure.

How BeMama can help

BeMama retains the source’s causes, inherited conditions, medicines, signs, testing, treatment, feeding and long-term effects while distinguishing acute encephalopathy from lasting kernicterus and removing universal thresholds, inevitable-outcome claims and feeding-only reassurance.

When to seek help

A jaundiced baby who is difficult to wake, not feeding, floppy or stiff, having abnormal movements or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency help. Temperature 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower, no wet nappies, or jaundice before 24 hours also requires immediate assessment. Do not wait for a feed or a scheduled test.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Common jaundice is different from acute bilirubin toxicity and lasting kernicterus.
  • Jaundice with poor waking, no feeding, abnormal tone or movements, breathing trouble, temperature extremes or no wet nappies needs immediate emergency care.
  • Age in hours, gestational age, serum bilirubin and individual risks guide treatment; colour and a universal cutoff do not.
  • Feeding support and timely follow-up are essential, but must not delay phototherapy or emergency specialist treatment.

Frequently asked questions

What causes kernicterus?

Severe unconjugated bilirubin exposure can injure the brain. Immature bilirubin handling, increased red-cell breakdown, inadequate intake, inherited disorders and illness can contribute. Jaundice alone does not mean brain injury; prompt testing and treatment reduce risk.

Which symptoms need emergency help?

With jaundice, unusual sleepiness or difficulty waking, no feeding, floppiness or stiffness, jerking or seizures, breathing difficulty, high-pitched crying or arching need immediate help. So do temperature 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower, no wet nappies, or jaundice in the first 24 hours.

Why does feeding matter?

Adequate milk intake supports hydration and bilirubin removal in stools. Feeding effectiveness and weight need assessment; supplementation may be necessary. More feeds are not a substitute for indicated phototherapy, and a baby not feeding needs emergency care.

What long-term problems can occur?

Movement and muscle-tone problems, hearing impairment, eye-movement difficulties, speech or coordination problems and enamel changes may occur; some children have learning difficulties. Effects vary, so specialist developmental and hearing assessment and individualized support are important.

Can a skin meter diagnose kernicterus?

No. It estimates bilirubin and can help decide when a blood test is needed. Serum results, the baby’s age and risks, examination and follow-up guide care; neither a skin reading nor a fixed number alone proves brain injury.

Can sunlight treat severe jaundice?

No. Sunlight is not a safe replacement for prescribed phototherapy. Do not delay urgent care for sunlight, herbs, water or sugar water.

Do all antibiotics cause kernicterus?

No. Risk depends on the medicine, exposure route and baby’s condition. Sulfonamides and G6PD-related haemolysis risks need review. Ask the clinician about infant or maternal prescriptions; do not give unprescribed antibiotics or stop necessary treatment yourself.

Can treatment reverse permanent injury?

Early treatment can prevent or limit damage, but established permanent injury cannot be promised to reverse. Acute signs are not a certain prediction of lasting disability; they demand immediate care and later individualized follow-up.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
